cards.title: AI is already in your pocket
cards.body:
Your phone unlocks when it sees your face. Your keyboard guesses the word you're about to type. A voice assistant turns what you say into text. Your music app suggests a song you end up loving.

All of these use **artificial intelligence**, or **AI**. In this course you'll find out what AI really is, how it learns and where it goes wrong, so you can use it well and spot its mistakes.

cards.title: Rules or examples?
cards.body:
Most programs follow **rules** that a person wrote, step by step. An alarm clock's rule is simple: at 7:00, ring.

Some jobs are far too hard to write rules for. Try writing rules for "what does my friend's face look like?" So instead, people give the computer lots of **examples** and let it work out what they have in common.

In this course, **AI** means software that learns from examples like this, instead of only following rules someone wrote.

cards.prompt: Does each one **follow rules** someone wrote, or **learn from examples**?

items.label: A spam filter that learns from you

cards.hint: Ask: could a person write down every step exactly? If yes, it follows rules.
cards.nudge: Look again at the jobs that have to cope with things nobody planned for, like a new photo of a face or a word you've never typed before.
cards.explanation: An alarm clock, a calculator and timed traffic lights follow exact rules someone wrote. Face unlock, a spam filter that learns from you and keyboard suggestions **learn from examples**: there are too many faces, emails and sentences to write rules for every one.

cards.title: Learning by example
cards.body:
Think about learning to cook. You could follow a recipe exactly, step by step. Or you could cook lots of meals, taste them and slowly learn what works.

Computers can learn the second way too. It's called **machine learning**: the computer is shown many examples and finds the patterns in them itself. Most of what people call AI today works like this.

cards.prompt: Which job is easiest to solve by **learning from examples**, instead of writing rules?

options.nudge: Adding follows exact rules that never change. Which job has too many different possibilities to write rules for?
That's one simple rule. Which job would need rules for millions of different cases?

options.text: Turning the lights off at midnight
options.nudge: A timer can do that with one rule. Think about a job where every example looks a bit different.

cards.hint: Which job has to cope with endless variety, where no two examples look exactly the same?
cards.explanation: Everyone's handwriting is different, so nobody could write rules for every way of writing every letter. Instead, a computer learns from thousands of handwriting examples. Adding up, alarms and timers each need just a few exact rules.

cards.prompt: Match each kind of [[AI|artificial-intelligence]] to the examples it learns from.
cards.hint: For each one, ask: what would it need to see lots of to get good at its job?
cards.nudge: Think about what each one is trying to guess, and which examples would show it the right answers.
cards.explanation: Song suggestions learn from what you **skip and replay**; face unlock from **scans of your face**; spam filters from emails people **mark as spam**; keyboards from the words people **usually type next**. Each one gets good at its job by seeing lots of examples of it.

cards.prompt: Trickier: does each one **follow rules**, or **learn from examples**?

items.label: A heater that learns when you're home
A game enemy on a set path
A game enemy trained on players
A photo app that finds dogs

cards.hint: Two things can do the same job in different ways. Look for words like "learns" and "trained", and ask whether someone could write every step.
cards.nudge: Some pairs look alike. Ask whether a person wrote the exact steps, or whether it got better by seeing examples.
cards.explanation: A timer, a set path and a unit converter follow exact rules. A heater that **learns** your routine, an enemy **trained** on players and a photo app that finds dogs all **learn from examples**. The same kind of job can be done either way.

cards.prompt: When [[AI|artificial-intelligence]] recognises your face, does it **understand** who you are, the way a friend does?

options.text: No: it matches patterns it learned from examples
Yes: it knows you like a friend does
options.nudge: A friend knows your jokes and your favourite food. What did the AI actually learn from?

options.text: Yes, but only on new phones
options.nudge: Newer phones are faster, but how the AI learned is the same. Does matching a face mean knowing the person?

options.text: No: it looks up your name online each time
options.nudge: It doesn't need to look anything up. Think about how it learned to recognise you.

cards.hint: Think back to how AI learns: from examples, finding what they have in common.
cards.explanation: Face unlock matches the **patterns** in your face to the examples it learned from. It doesn't know who you are, what you like or how you feel. That's a big difference between AI and people, and it's why AI can be fooled or make odd mistakes.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Ordinary programs follow **rules** a person wrote.
- **AI** learns from **examples** instead, finding patterns in them. This is called **machine learning**.
- AI is everywhere: face unlock, keyboard suggestions, spam filters, song suggestions.
- It matches patterns. It doesn't understand things the way people do.

Next: you'll teach a model yourself.
